title: Xsight Labs E1L DPU for Lower-Power 200Gbps DPUs
gist: Xsight Labs announced the E1L DPU, a lower-power version of its 64-core E1 with 8, 16 or 22 Arm Neoverse N2 cores, up to 200Gbps and 25-40W TDP, suited to network switches via COM Express Type 7. STH frames it as the anti-AMD Pensando, relying on standard Linux and DPDK on vanilla Arm cores.

insights.claim: The Xsight Labs E1L DPU brings 8, 16 or 22 Arm Neoverse N2 cores into a power envelope low enough for network switches or other low-power footprints, as a lower-power alternative to the 64-core E1.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Extends Xsight's Arm DPU design downmarket to power-constrained uses.
insights.locator: The new Xsight Labs E1L DPU

insights.claim: The E1L offers up to 200Gbps over 4 SerDes lanes, up to 2 DDR5-5200 interfaces with inline encryption, line-rate AES-GCM for IPsec offload and 20 PCIe Gen5 lanes across 6 dual-mode controllers with SR-IOV.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: I/O and crypto capabilities cover infrastructure offload use cases.

insights.claim: The E1L has configurable TDPs of 25W, 30W and 40W, with typical draw of 15W, 18W and 25W respectively.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Low typical power enables placement inside switches and storage servers.

insights.claim: The E1L is designed to run on a COM Express Type 7 module, which the author says works in network switches and is also interesting for NVMe and disk storage servers.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Module form factor eases integration into switches and storage platforms.
insights.locator: The new DPU is designed to run

insights.claim: Xsight's approach is the 'anti-AMD Pensando': AMD says running network offloads via Linux and DPDK on many Arm cores is the wrong approach and favors P4 programmable engines, while Xsight runs on vanilla Arm cores.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Two opposing DPU architecture philosophies are competing: programmable pipelines versus general-purpose Arm.
insights.locator: Xsight's idea is basically the anti-AMD Pensando

insights.claim: Xsight's Neoverse N2 implementation is so vanilla that STH installed out-of-the-box Ubuntu LTS on the 64-core E1 DPU, and using DPDK and standard Linux means acceleration should scale down easily from the 800Gbps E1 to the E1L.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Standard software compatibility lowers adoption friction.
insights.locator: The Neoverse N2 cores on the E1 DPU

insights.claim: While much of the industry chases 800Gbps and higher, Xsight is scaling its 800Gbps design down to 200Gbps and lower power, opening applications where power matters more than peak speed.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A differentiated niche exists in lower-speed, lower-power DPUs.

insights.claim: STH charted single-core Neoverse N2 results on its AgentSTH V7 workloads and Geekbench 5 against NVIDIA's BlueField-2; the E1's large multi-core delta is partly due to having 64 cores and a newer architecture.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Comparison with older BlueField-2 is not like for like.

insights.claim: The author considers an 8-22 core part very capable for storage, switch control planes and virtualization hosts, and notes E1.L SSDs could theoretically attach to the E1L's PCIe lanes to build a system around E1L/E1.L.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Target use cases are control-plane and storage nodes rather than peak throughput.
